claim: Barrington's nucleus is also known as the pontine micturition centre.
source: Barrington's nucleus, also known as the pontine micturition centre, is a key site for the control of urination (Barrington, 1925).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with a citation to Barrington, 1925.

claim: Lesions of Barrington's nucleus abolish micturition.
source: Lesions of Barrington's nucleus (Barrington, 1925) or acute transection of the pons abolishes micturition (De Groat, 1975; Sadananda et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Supra-collicular decerebration or transection of PAG does not stop micturition in cats, rats or mice.
source: In contrast, supra-collicular decerebration or transection of PAG does not stop micturition in cats, rats or mice (Takasaki et al., 2010; Sadananda et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in multiple species.

claim: Co-ordinated voiding is seen under anaesthesia when the contextual element of volitional voiding is removed.
source: Similarly, co-ordinated voiding is seen under anaesthesia (Pavcovich and Valentino, 1995; Hou et al., 2016; Ito et al., 2017; Keller et al., 2018; Verstegen et al., 2019) when the contextual element of volitional voiding is removed.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating voiding under anaesthesia.

claim: One of the largest populations of Barrington's nucleus neurons expresses corticotropin releasing hormone (CRH) in humans and rodents.
source: One of the largest populations of Barrington's nucleus neurons expresses corticotropin releasing hormone (CRH) in humans (Ruggiero et al., 1999) and rodents (Vincent and Satoh, 1984; Valentino et al., 1995; Valentino et al., 2011; Verstegen et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies in humans and rodents.

claim: BarrCRH neuron axons terminate in the vicinity of the sacral parasympathetic neurons.
source: and their axons terminate in the vicinity of the sacral parasympathetic neurons (Valentino et al., 2011; Hou et al., 2016; Verstegen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical tracing studies.

claim: BarrCRH neurons are glutamatergic.
source: These studies indicated that BarrCRH neurons were glutamatergic, their activation caused bladder contraction (Hou et al., 2016; Keller et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation of BarrCRH neurons causes bladder contraction.
source: These studies indicated that BarrCRH neurons were glutamatergic, their activation caused bladder contraction (Hou et al., 2016; Keller et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous optogenetic studies.

claim: Increasing BarrCRH neuron excitability increases the probability of micturition.
source: and increasing their excitability increased the probability of micturition (Verstegen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a chemogenetic study.

claim: BarrESR1 neurons are important for control of the urethral sphincter in voluntary scent marking with urine.
source: A second smaller subgroup of oestrogen receptor type-1 positive neurons in Barrington's nucleus (BarrESR1) have been shown to be important for control of the urethral sphincter in voluntary scent marking with urine (Keller et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on BarrESR1 neurons.

claim: Layer-5 pyramidal neurons in the primary motor cortex play a role in the descending control of voluntary urination via their projections to Barrington's nucleus.
source: Further a group of layer-5 pyramidal neurons in the primary motor cortex plays a role in the descending control of voluntary urination via their projections to Barrington's nucleus (Yao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on cortical control.

claim: Tonic unilateral activation of BarrCRH neurons increases micturition frequency.
source: Tonic unilateral activation of BarrCRH neurons (5–20 Hz x 20 ms, 465 nm light pulses, applied for three completed voiding cycles) produced an increase of micturition frequency (to 153.2 ± 15.6% of basal after 10 Hz stimulation, Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Tonic unilateral activation of BarrCRH neurons reduces the threshold pressure for voiding.
source: manifesting as a significant shortening in inter-void interval associated with a reduction of the threshold pressure for voiding (84.0 ± 4.7% at 10 Hz, Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of BarrCRH neurons produces a prolonged reduction in the frequency of voids during continuous infusion protocol.
source: Administration of Clozapine N-oxide (CNO, 5 mg/kg i.p) produced a prolonged reduction in the frequency of voids seen during a continuous infusion protocol (reduced to 66.8 ± 6.3% of control at 20 mins, Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of BarrCRH neurons increases threshold pressure, fill volume and micturition pressure.
source: This was associated with increases of threshold pressure, fill volume and micturition pressure (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of BarrCRH neurons using a fill and hold protocol produces a prolongation of the latency to void, effectively producing urinary retention.
source: Using this protocol, chemogenetic inhibition caused a prolongation of the latency to void (from 207 ± 17 s at baseline to 738 ± 60 s at 20mins after CNO). This effectively produced a period of urinary retention, that persisted for 2 hr (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Unilateral opto-activation of BarrCRH neurons evokes non-voiding contractions of the bladder (eNVC) when the bladder is filled to half of its threshold capacity.
source: In initial experiments, unilateral opto-activation of BarrCRH (20 ms x 20 Hz for 5 s) evoked non-voiding contractions of the bladder (eNVC, Figure 3A and B, with the bladder filled to half of its threshold capacity, n = 7 mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Varying stimulus frequencies and pulse durations produces modestly graded changes in eNVC with a 20 ms x 20 Hz protocol producing near maximal responses.
source: Varying stimulus frequencies and pulse durations produced modestly graded changes in eNVC with a 20 ms x 20 Hz protocol producing near maximal responses (3.9 ± 0.8 mmHg, Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The eNVC had a consistent latency to onset of 1.3 ± 0.1 s and a time to peak of 6.0 ± 0.3 s following stimulus onset and an average duration of 8.2 ± 0.6 s.
source: The eNVC had a consistent latency to onset of 1.3 ± 0.1 s and a time to peak of 6.0 ± 0.3 s following stimulus onset and an average duration of 8.2 ± 0.6 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: With each of the stimulus parameters there were 'failures' where there was no detectable bladder response.
source: With each of the stimulus parameters there were 'failures' where there was no detectable bladder response (Figure 3 and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3 and E.

claim: The probability of eNVC increases with stimulation frequency, with 20 Hz being the most reliable.
source: The probability of eNVC increased with stimulation frequency (71.4 ± 7.6% at 2.5 Hz and 97.1 ± 2.5% at 20 Hz) with 20 Hz being the most reliable.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Single light pulses of longer duration (1–3 s) are able to reliably generate eNVC.
source: Single light pulses of longer duration (1–3 s) were also able to reliably generate eNVC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Optogenetic activation of BarrCRH neurons does not alter distal colonic pressure.
source: Furthermore, optogenetic activation of BarrCRH neurons did not alter distal colonic pressure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), despite the generation of bladder eNVC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Bilateral activation of BarrCRH produces larger eNVC than optoactivation of either side alone.
source: Bilateral activation of BarrCRH produced larger eNVC (7.1 ± 2.0 mmHg at 20 ms and 20 Hz, n = 7 mice) than optoactivation of either side alone (2.9 ± 0.5 and 3.1 ± 0.8 mmHg for right or left side, respectively), particularly at higher frequencies of stimulation (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: The effect of bilateral stimulation on eNVC amplitude is additive rather than synergistic.
source: The effect of bilateral stimulation on eNVC amplitude was additive rather than synergistic.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing unilateral and bilateral stimulation.

claim: The probability of generating eNVC is increased by bilateral stimulation.
source: The probability of generating eNVC was increased by bilateral stimulation (evident at lower stimulus frequencies that is increased by 154 ± 18% for bilateral vs right alone or by 158 ± 17% for bilateral vs left alone at 2.5 Hz, Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: With the bladder filled to half of its threshold capacity, bilateral BarrCRH stimulation never triggered voids.
source: It was notable that, with the bladder filled to half of its threshold capacity, bilateral BarrCRH stimulation never triggered voids.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: The amplitude of BarrCRH eNVC increases progressively through the micturition cycle during continuous bladder filling.
source: During continuous bladder filling, it was noted that the amplitude of BarrCRH eNVC increased progressively through the micturition cycle (increase of 17.0 ± 3.9 fold, comparing eNVC obtained during the 2nd versus 5th quintile of micturition cycle, Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–D.

claim: The probability of obtaining a bladder contraction with optoactivation increases with progressive filling, with most 'failures' being seen when the bladder is <40% filled.
source: Similarly, the probability of obtaining a bladder contraction with optoactivation also increased with progressive filling, with most 'failures' being seen when the bladder was <40% filled (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Pelvic nerve stimulation in the pithed decerebrate, arterially-perfused mouse preparation shows that the amplitude of bladder contractions increases with bladder filling but plateaus at a volume of ~50 µl.
source: The amplitude of bladder contractions induced by pelvic nerve stimulation (4–20 Hz, 10V, 3 s) increased with bladder filling (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) with a doubling (2.2 ± 0.34 fold at 20 Hz) of the pressure generated between empty bladder and 70 µl fill (close to voiding threshold in an intact mouse). However, this amplitude increase plateaued at a volume of ~50 µl
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: It is possible to trigger fully co-ordinated voids by activating BarrCRH neurons later in the cycle (>50% filled).
source: However, by applying stimuli systematically at points through the micturition cycle it was possible to trigger fully co-ordinated voids by activating BarrCRH neurons later in the cycle (>50% filled, Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: The pattern and amplitude of the evoked bladder contraction is similar to that seen with spontaneous voids.
source: The pattern and amplitude of the evoked bladder contraction was similar to that seen with spontaneous voids and they occurred at a similar latency to eNVC.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental data.

claim: BarrCRH eNVC are never associated with EUS activity irrespective of their magnitude.
source: The BarrCRH eNVC (irrespective of their magnitude) were never associated with EUS activity (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5B and D.

claim: When BarrCRH activation evokes a voiding contraction, bursting EUS activity is always found.
source: However, when BarrCRH activation evoked a voiding contraction then bursting EUS activity was always found (Figure 5D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5D and F.

claim: BarrCRH induced voids have EUS activity that is indistinguishable from spontaneous voids in terms of burst duration and frequency.
source: These BarrCRH induced voids had EUS activity that was indistinguishable from spontaneous voids in terms of burst duration (spontaneous 4.4 ± 0.9 vs opto-induced 4.4 ± 1.0 s, n = 7, paired t-test, ns) and frequency (spontaneous 22.7 ± 2.7 vs opto-induced 21.5 ± 3.0 Hz, n = 7, paired t-test, ns)).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing spontaneous and opto-induced voids.

claim: BarrCRH axons provide a specific innervation of the sacral parasympathetic neurons but not to the ventral horn at the level of Onuf's nucleus.
source: The axons from BarrCRH were noted to provide a specific innervation of the sacral parasympathetic neurons but not to the ventral horn at the level of Onuf's nucleus (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Optogenetic stimuli applied to the spinal cord reliably induce bladder contractions.
source: Optogenetic stimuli (either 20 ms x 20 Hz for 5 s or single 1 s pulse) applied to the spinal cord reliably induced bladder contractions (Figure 6B–D, p=0.025, bladder half filled).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: eNVCs evoked by spinal activation tend to occur with a shorter latency than those evoked directly from pontine stimulation.
source: These eNVCs tended to occur with a shorter latency than those evoked directly from pontine stimulation (1.0 ± 0.2 s vs 1.26 ± 0.1 s, n = 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing latencies.

claim: During continuous bladder filling, spinal activation can trigger full voids.
source: Similarly, during continuous bladder filling, spinal activation could trigger full voids (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Intrathecal Astressin significantly and reversibly increases the amplitude of eNVC, an action that is more pronounced as the bladder fills.
source: Counter to the prediction, Astressin significantly and reversibly increased the amplitude of eNVC, an action that was more pronounced as the bladder filled (333 ± 75%, p=0.008 (n = 7), 20 mins after Astressin, Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Intrathecal Astressin decreases the infused volume required to trigger a void.
source: Intrathecal Astressin also decreased the infused volume required to trigger a void (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: CRH provides a negative feedback signal to limit the extent of the spinal parasympathetic response to BarrCRH neuronal activity.
source: This indicates that CRH is providing a negative feedback signal to limit the extent of the spinal parasympathetic response to BarrCRH neuronal activity (in agreement with Pavcovich and Valentino, 1995; Kiddoo et al., 2006; Wood et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the Astressin data and is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A total of 113 individual neurons were identified by clustering from recordings made in the vicinity of Barrington's nucleus.
source: A total of 113 individual neurons were identified by clustering from recordings made in the vicinity of Barrington's nucleus (n = 3 mice, Figure 8BD).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental recordings and analysis.

claim: Definitive opto-identification of BarrCRH neurons (n = 12) was indicated by reliable short latency spike entrainment to light with time-locked, maintained firing in response to longer light pulses.
source: Definitive opto-identification of BarrCRH neurons (n = 12) was indicated by reliable short latency spike entrainment to light (20 ms pulses, Figure 8C) with time-locked, maintained firing in response to longer light pulses (≥1 s, Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental criteria for optogenetic identification shown in Figure 8C.

claim: BarrCRH neurons show a characteristic pattern of activity during the micturition cycle with bursting at the time of voiding.
source: These BarrCRH neurons showed a characteristic pattern of activity during the micturition cycle with bursting at the time of voiding (Figure 9A, 20.5 ± 4.1 Hz peak firing frequency).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings shown in Figure 9A.

claim: A second population of neurons termed BarrCRH-like (n = 32) was recorded with a similar pattern of activity to BarrCRH neurons but were not activated by light.
source: A second population of neurons was recorded with a similar pattern of activity (but were not activated by light) that are henceforth termed BarrCRH-like (n = 32, Figures 9B and 10A,B)
evidence: This claim is based on experimental recordings and classification.

claim: BarrCRH-like neurons have a short-latency synchrony with the BarrCRH neurons that is evident in cross-correlograms.
source: These BarrCRH-like neurons had a short-latency synchrony with the BarrCRH neurons that was evident in cross-correlograms (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both BarrCRH and BarrCRH-like neurons show a clear temporal relationship to bladder pressure with their firing preceding and ramping up with the pressure during voiding.
source: Both BarrCRH and BarrCRH-like neurons showed a clear temporal relationship to bladder pressure (Figure 9C) with their firing preceding and ramping up with the pressure during voiding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings shown in Figure 9C.

claim: For both the BarrCRH and BarrCRH-like neurons there is a strong sigmoid relationship between bladder pressure and neuronal firing.
source: For both the BarrCRH and BarrCRH-like neurons there was a strong sigmoid relationship between bladder pressure and neuronal firing (Figure 10C), which wasnot seen in the non-identified group of neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental analysis shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The increases in firing frequency for both BarrCRH and BarrCRH-like neurons precede increases in bladder pressure by ~3 s.
source: The directionality of this influence was investigated by examining the cross-correlation between firing rate and bladder pressure – this indicated that the increases in firing frequency (for both BarrCRH and BarrCRH-like neurons) preceded increases in bladder pressure by ~3 s for both sets of neurons (Figure 10D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental analysis shown in Figure 10D.

claim: LC neurons increase their firing around the void but this peri-void activation is significantly less pronounced than the increase in firing seen in the BarrCRH-like and BarrCRH neurons.
source: LC cells increased their firing around the void – a pattern that was evident in individual firing rate plots and in the z-scored firing heatmap (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A and B). However this peri-void activation was significantly less pronounced than the increase in firing seen in the BarrCRH-like (and BarrCRH) neurons (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: During all phases of the voiding cycle it is possible to opto-excite BarrCRH neurons and the increase in firing frequency is independent of the phase of the micturition cycle.
source: During all phases of the voiding cycle it was possible to opto-excite BarrCRH neurons (Figure 11A) and the increase in firing frequency in both absolute and relative terms was independent of the phase of the micturition cycle (Figure 11B, ranging from 22.4 ± 7.7 to 24.0 ± 6.5 Hz across micturition phases).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11A and B.

claim: The intrinsic excitability of the BarrCRH neurons does not vary across the micturition cycle.
source: These data indicate that the intrinsic excitability of the BarrCRH neurons does not vary across the micturition cycle and that augmentation of the bladder pressure responses (by 17.0 ± 3.9 fold) occurs downstream of the firing output from Barrington's nucleus.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing constant opto-evoked firing across cycle phases.

claim: A burst of firing in the BarrCRH neurons precedes spontaneous non-voiding contractions (sNVC) by 1.5–3.0 s.
source: A burst of firing in the BarrCRH neurons preceded the sNVC by 1.5–3.0 s – suggesting that they were triggered by a signal from the pons (Figure 11C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental analysis shown in Figure 11C and D.

claim: There is only a weak relationship between the magnitude of each BarrCRH burst and the amplitude of the associated sNVC.
source: However, there was only a weak relationship between the magnitude of each BarrCRH burst and the amplitude of the associated sNVC (see Figure 11E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental analysis shown in Figure 11E.

claim: A linear fit of the data indicates that an increase in burst size of 20 spikes would only account for 0.5 mmHg difference in sNVC size (less than 20% of the observed range of amplitudes).
source: A linear fit of these data indicates that an increase in burst size of 20 spikes (close to the maximum observed range) would only account for 0.5 mmHg difference in sNVC size (less than 20% of the observed range of amplitudes).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The incrementing frequency of afferent drive as the bladder fills leads to summation and a maintained membrane depolarisation that increases parasympathetic excitability in the NEURON model.
source: The incrementing frequency of afferent drive, as the bladder fills, leads to summation and a maintained membrane depolarisation that increases parasympathetic excitability (Figure 12B).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 12B.

claim: The NEURON model shows that the output from the parasympathetic neuron when driven by BarrCRH is strongly dependent upon the phase of the micturition cycle with a ~10 fold increase over the voiding cycle.
source: The resulting output from the parasympathetic neuron when driven by BarrCRH (with a mimicked 20 Hz optogenetic drive) was strongly dependent upon the phase of the micturition cycle with a ~ 10 fold increase over the voiding cycle which closely parallels the experimental data.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: In the early phase of the voiding cycle the BarrCRH input is unable to evoke action potentials in the NEURON model, thus producing 'failures'.
source: Note also that in the early phase of the voiding cycle the BarrCRH input is unable to evoke action potentials – thus producing 'failures'.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: The integrated model of autonomous micturition closely reproduces characteristics of the observed micturition cycle with graded NVCs, periodic voids and patterns of BarrCRH firing.
source: The resulting feedback loop (depicted schematically in Figure 13B) closely reproduces characteristic of the observed micturition cycle with graded NVCs, periodic voids and patterns of BarrCRH firing.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 13B.

claim: Attenuation of the variance in BarrCRH firing delays the time to void in the model, indicating the importance of NVCs in the process.
source: In line with experimental data, attenuation of the variance in BarrCRH firing (underpinning the NVCs) delays the time to void – indicating their importance in the process (Figure 13—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 13—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Augmenting the spinal parasympathetic sensitivity to the BarrCRH drive in the model increases the amplitude of the NVCs and shortens the inter-void interval.
source: Similarly, augmenting the spinal parasympathetic sensitivity to the BarrCRH drive (as seen experimentally with intrathecal Astressin) increases the amplitude of the NVCs and shortens the inter-void interval (Figure 13—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 13—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Simulated optogenetic drive of BarrCRH neurons in the model produces both failures, eNVCs and triggers voids earlier in the cycle than would otherwise have happened.
source: This effect is demonstrated with the simulated optogenetic drive of BarrCRH neurons (20 Hz x 1 s, Figure 13—figure supplement 1B) which produces both failures, eNVCs and triggers voids earlier in the cycle than would otherwise have happened.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 13—figure supplement 1B.

claim: BarrCRH neurons do not simply act as high-fidelity controllers of bladder pressure but play a more nuanced, probabilistic role.
source: These findings indicate that BarrCRH neurons do play a critical role in micturition. However, the activity of BarrCRH neurons, is not a simple switch mechanism for voiding nor do they provide a direct drive to bladder pressure (as might be expected for an autonomic command neuron). Instead these neurons play a more nuanced, probabilistic role.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The influence of BarrCRH neurons on the bladder depends on the state of priming of the downstream parasympathetic motor circuit.
source: Their influence on the bladder depends on the state of priming of the downstream parasympathetic motor circuit.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: BarrCRH neurons are the efferent limb of an inferential circuit that assays bladder state repeatedly during the storage phase of the cycle.
source: This identifies the BarrCRH neurons as being the efferent limb of an inferential circuit that assays bladder state repeatedly during the storage phase of the cycle.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings and modeling.

claim: When the threshold for voiding is reached, BarrCRH neurons generate a high-fidelity motor signal through a positive feedback loop that drives the bladder contraction required for voiding.
source: When the threshold for voiding is reached, they generate a high-fidelity motor signal through a positive feedback loop that drives the bladder contraction required for voiding.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings and modeling.

claim: Dysfunction of the descending control system from Barrington's nucleus, as seen following spinal cord injury, results in a loss of voluntary control and initially in a complete loss of continence.
source: Dysfunction of this descending control system, as is seen following spinal cord injury, results in a loss of voluntary control and initially in a complete loss of continence, but this tends to be restored as the spinal micturition reflex re-emerges (albeit in a poorly co-ordinated manner).
evidence: This claim is based on established clinical knowledge.

claim: Urethane has been adopted by many research groups as the anaesthetic agent producing the least autonomic suppression and for its stable plane of anaesthesia.
source: Urethane has been adopted by many research groups as the agent producing the least autonomic suppression and for its stable plane of anaesthesia.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The cystometric profile and the characteristic activity of the EUS seen in this study is akin to that seen in awake mice and in decerebrate arterially perfused preparations in the absence of anaesthesia.
source: The cystometric profile and the characteristic activity of the EUS seen in this study is akin to that seen in awake mice and in decerebrate arterially perfused preparations in the absence of anaesthesia (Ito et al., 2017; Ito et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Male mice use strategic urine 'spotting' to express their dominance and territorial ownership.
source: Rodents also use social urine scent marking, for example male mice use strategic urine 'spotting' to express their dominance and territorial ownership (Desjardins et al., 1973; Maruniak et al., 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: There are differences in the patterns of urination between autonomous micturition and scent marking with greater frequency and smaller volumes in each urine spot compared to a primary void.
source: Although autonomous micturition and scent marking with urine are related processes, likely with some shared physiology, there are also differences in the patterns of urination with greater frequency (>10 urine spots per minute Keller et al., 2018) and accordingly smaller volumes in each urine spot compared to a primary void (typically 80–120 ul) (Yu et al., 2014; Bjorling et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2018; Ito et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BarrESR1 neurons preferentially target a spinal inter-neuronal circuit that is proposed to be involved in generating the bursting drive to the EUS as well as causing a bladder contraction.
source: These BarrESR1 neurons preferentially target a spinal inter-neuronal circuit that is proposed to be involved in generating the bursting drive to the EUS as well as causing a bladder contraction.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited studies.

claim: The majority of spinally projecting Barr neurons are CRH positive.
source: This is somewhat surprising given that the majority of spinally projecting Barr neurons are CRH positive (Verstegen et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an anatomical study.

claim: Genetic, diphtheria toxin-mediated, ablation of the BarrCRH neurons produces a phenotype of increased voided volume in awake mice and markedly delayed voiding during cystometry in anaesthetised mice.
source: With hindsight, a clue to this puzzle may have been offered by the finding of Verstegen et al. (2019) that genetic, diphtheria toxin-mediated, ablation of the BarrCRH neurons produced a phenotype of increased voided volume in awake mice and markedly delayed voiding during cystometry in anaesthetised mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: There are parallel pathways from Barrington's nucleus to the downstream spinal pattern generators: the BarrESR1 neurons driving spotting behaviour and the BarrCRH neurons which conditionally requires the bladder to be distended before a void can be generated.
source: Given the mechanistic differences between the processes of autonomous micturition and voluntary scent marking in males, it is quite likely that there are distinct circuit drives for each type of urination. This would be consistent with the proposition that there are parallel pathways from Barrington's nucleus to the downstream spinal pattern generators: the BarrESR1 neurons driving spotting behaviour which can be triggered irrespective of the degree of fullness of the male mouse bladder; and the other mediated by BarrCRH neurons which conditionally requires the bladder to be distended before a void can be generated.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings and previous studies.

claim: Female mice have smaller bladder capacities along with larger basal and micturition pressures on CMG compared to males but there are no differences in other parameters and their EUS-EMG trace is qualitatively similar in pattern during voiding.
source: Our study did not set out to identify gender differences in BarrCRH neuronal function in micturition and we included mice of both sexes. Although female mice had smaller bladder capacities along with larger basal and micturition pressures on CMG there were no differences in their other parameters and their EUS-EMG trace was qualitatively similar in pattern during voiding.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: Both sexes show similar responses to activation/inhibition of BarrCRH neurons.
source: Equally both sexes showed similar responses to activation/inhibition of BarrCRH neurons which presumably relates to underlying commonalities in the processes of autonomous micturition.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: Humans and cats do not show the same 'squirting' behaviour as their EUS relaxes to allow voiding, which likely involves some distinctive neuronal circuitry.
source: In this context it is also important to acknowledge that the pattern of micturition varies to a degree across species and humans and cats do not show the same 'squirting' behaviour as their EUS relaxes to allow voiding – this likely involves some distinctive neuronal circuitry (Fowler et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: The time taken to void is surprisingly similar irrespective of body size, indicating that many of the fundamental principles of operation are conserved.
source: However, there are also many similarities including, surprisingly, in the time taken to void irrespective of body size (Yang et al., 2014) indicating that many of the fundamental principles of operation are conserved.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a comparative study.

claim: Lesions or inhibition of Barrington's nucleus abolishes voiding in multiple species including humans, cats, rats and mice.
source: Importantly, lesions or inhibition of Barrington's nucleus abolishes voiding in multiple species including humans, cats, rats and mice consistent with it being a core circuit component reviewed in Verstegen et al. (2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: The pattern of firing activity seen in optogenetically-identified BarrCRH neurons in anaesthetised mice is similar to that previously noted in recordings from Barrington's nucleus in the conscious rat.
source: The pattern of firing activity seen here in optogenetically-identified BarrCRH neurons in anaesthetised mice is similar to that previously noted in recordings from Barrington's nucleus in the conscious rat (Manohar et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The pattern of firing activity in BarrCRH neurons is reminiscent of a subset of the neurons identified in anaesthetised or decerebrate rats and cats that showed a ramping activity with voiding.
source: and is also reminiscent of a subset of the neurons identified in anaesthetised or decerebrate rats and cats that showed a ramping activity with voiding (de Groat et al., 1998; Sugaya et al., 2003; Tanaka et al., 2003; Sasaki, 2005b; Sasaki, 2005a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In none of the recordings from BarrCRH or any of the neurons in the vicinity was any pattern of activity seen that resembled the high frequency bursting of the urethral sphincter seen in mice and rats.
source: It is also worth noting that in none of these recordings (from BarrCRH or indeed any of the neurons in the vicinity) was any pattern of activity seen that resembled the high frequency bursting of the urethral sphincter seen in mice and rats – to date such activity has never been observed in any of the recordings from Barrington's nucleus
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: The high frequency bursting of the urethral sphincter is generated from a spinal motor pattern generator such as the LSCC.
source: which is consistent with the idea that it is generated from a spinal motor pattern generator such as the LSCC (Chang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and is supported by a citation.

claim: Previous electrical stimulation studies of Barrington's nucleus in the rat indicated that the degree of excitation of the parasympathetic motor outflow to the bladder was strongly dependent upon the degree of bladder filling.
source: In support of this idea, previous electrical stimulation studies of Barrington's nucleus in the rat indicated that the degree of excitation of the parasympathetic motor outflow to the bladder was strongly dependent upon the degree of bladder filling (Noto et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: An increase in the frequency and amplitude of NVCs has been linked to diseases of the LUT.
source: An increase in their frequency and amplitude has been linked to diseases of the LUT (Vahabi and Drake, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a clinical study.

claim: An increase in the frequency and amplitude of NVCs is associated with loss of descending control from the brainstem.
source: and also with loss of descending control from the brainstem (Sadananda et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: There is evidence of peripheral generation of NVCs by the bladder early in development which becomes less coordinated in adult bladder.
source: There is also evidence of their peripheral generation by the bladder early in development which becomes less coordinated in adult bladder (Kanai et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a developmental study.

claim: NVCs are generated by the 'noisy' probabilistic drive from Barrington's nucleus that repeatedly assesses the status of the spinal circuit during each micturition cycle.
source: We provide evidence that NVCs are generated by the 'noisy' probabilistic drive from Barrington's nucleus that repeatedly assesses the status of the spinal circuit during each micturition cycle and that the magnitude of the bladder pressure response reflects the phase of the micturition cycle.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The resulting afferent signal from NVCs provides an active way of inferring the degree of bladder fullness.
source: The resulting afferent signal provides an active way of inferring the degree of bladder fullness (analogous to the 'sampling' that assesses rectal fullness Rao, 2004)
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings and is supported by an analogy to rectal sampling.

claim: The afferent signal from NVCs could prime the neural control circuits and could conceivably provide a stream of information that may enable a conscious awareness of bladder fullness and the ability to make volitional predictions about the need to void.
source: and could prime the neural control circuits and indeed could conceivably provide a stream of information that may enable a conscious awareness of bladder fullness and the ability to make volitional predictions about the need to void.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on inference from the findings.

claim: There is homology with the development of other motor systems where spontaneous motor activity, initially generated in the periphery, becomes progressively embedded centrally as motor representations in the nervous system with developmental maturation.
source: We also note the homology with the development of other motor systems where spontaneous motor activity, initially generated in the periphery, becomes progressively embedded centrally as motor representations in the nervous system with developmental maturation (Llinás, 2001).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and is supported by a citation to a theoretical framework.

claim: A direct volitional drive to BarrCRH from cortex would not be subject to the probabilistic firing switch at a supraspinal level and could therefore trigger a void earlier in the cycle if behaviourally appropriate.
source: A feature of this circuit organisation is that a direct volitional drive to BarrCRH from cortex as recently reported (Yao et al., 2018) would not be subject to the probabilistic firing switch at a supraspinal level and could therefore trigger a void earlier in the cycle if behaviourally appropriate albeit still contingent on the priming status of the spinal gate.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the model and is supported by a citation.

claim: A parallel synaptic drive from the BarrESR1 neurons that is stronger than the BarrCRH neurons could generate parasympathetic activity without requiring co-incident afferent activity, hence bypassing the gate to produce urine 'spotting' on behavioural demand.
source: Hypothetically, a parallel synaptic drive from the BarrESR1 neurons (Keller et al., 2018) that was stronger than the BarrCRH neurons could also generate parasympathetic activity without requiring co-incident afferent activity – hence bypassing the gate to produce urine 'spotting' on behavioural demand.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on inference and is supported by a citation.

claim: The BarrCRH neurons form a key component of the micturition circuit that generate a pre-motor drive to the bladder late in the cycle.
source: On this basis we conclude that the BarrCRH neurons form a key component of the micturition circuit that generate a pre-motor drive to the bladder late in the cycle.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The drive from BarrCRH neurons is not generated by a burst generator residing within this cell population but is a product of the integration of inputs from both bladder sensory afferents and upstream centres such as the PAG, hypothalamus and motor cortex.
source: The recording and stimulation data suggest that this drive is not generated by a burst generator residing within this cell population but is a product of the integration of inputs from both bladder sensory afferents and upstream centres such as the PAG but also including hypothalamus and motor cortex (Hou et al., 2016; Yao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings and is supported by citations.

claim: Failures of control at the BarrCRH locus are likely to be involved in both acute disorders of lower urinary tract function such as retention as well as in chronic diseases like nocturnal enuresis, detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia and overactive bladder syndrome.
source: We predict that failures of control at this key integrating locus are likely to be involved in both acute disorders of lower urinary tract function such as retention as well as in chronic diseases like nocturnal enuresis, detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia and overactive bladder syndrome where there is dysregulation of detrusor contractions and sphincter relaxation.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on inference from the findings.
